name: Frontal-orbital advancement (frontal bossing / brow)

lead: Frontal-orbital advancement, also called frontal bossing, is the goal of moving the brow ridge and upper orbital area forward. The payoff people want is a more prominent, masculine upper face and eyes that look more deep-set under a strong brow.

The nearest documented surgery is facial feminization, which usually reduces the brow ridge by grinding or reshaping bone over the frontal sinus, and brow lifts, which change eyebrow position rather than bone projection. Looksmaxxing forum discussion centres on brow lifts and combined surgery trips; no study of cosmetic advancement in people without a craniofacial condition was found.

paras: People pursue this through consultations with craniofacial or facial plastic surgeons, often as part of a larger multi-procedure plan. Brow lifts reposition soft tissue, while bone work reshapes the forehead. Healing takes weeks to months before the final shape is visible.

Cranioplasty-type bone surgery carries risks of improper bone healing, bone fragment movement and cyst formation, and thin sinus walls complicate bone work near the forehead. Outcome data for forehead and orbit procedures are limited. It is major surgery under general anaesthesia, so surgeon experience and a realistic consultation matter.

web.title: Advancements in facial implantology: a review of hydroxyapatite applications and outcomes

angle.text: The aim is a more projected brow and forehead, which gives a stronger, more masculine upper face and deeper-set eyes. It works by moving the brow ridge and upper orbit forward, or by repositioning brow tissue. Published surgery covers brow lifts and brow reduction rather than cosmetic advancement.

lead: Frontal-orbital advancement and frontal bossing, as the terms appear in looksmaxxing, describe a more forward-projecting brow ridge and upper orbital rim, along with a fuller forehead. Members of looks-focused communities discuss this projection as part of an 'eye area' aesthetic, where a prominent supraorbital ridge shades the eyes and is linked to what they call hunter eyes.[1] Some describe pursuing it through supraorbital implants, bone-cement augmentation or related craniofacial surgery, while others argue that midface and under-eye support matter more.[1]

The terminology comes from clinical practice. Fronto-orbital advancement is an established operation in paediatric craniofacial surgery, where the bony bar above the eyes and the frontal bone are moved forward to treat conditions such as craniosynostosis.[2] Frontal bossing is a medical term for a protruding forehead, which clinicians describe in connection with growth-hormone excess, rickets, chronic anaemia and a range of genetic syndromes.[3][4] In forums the terms are borrowed to describe a cosmetic goal.

How the forward brow is meant to look better: proponents of the aesthetic say a projecting upper orbital rim casts shadow across the eyes, shortens the apparent distance between brow and lash line, and gives the upper third of the face a firmer, more angular outline, which they associate with a masculine profile and with the hunter-eye look.[1] Clinicians working on the forehead describe a related principle from the other direction: in feminization surgery the brow ridge is treated as one of the main cues of facial sex, so changing its projection visibly changes how the upper face reads.[5][6]

The nearest published cosmetic literature concerns the opposite direction: facial feminization surgery, which reduces the male brow ridge and reshapes the forehead,[5][6] and brow-lift procedures that change eyebrow position rather than bone projection.[7][8][9] No published study has examined elective forward advancement of the brow and orbit for appearance in people without a craniofacial condition.
infobox: Fronto-orbital advancement (craniosynostosis surgery, usually age 6-12 months)[2]
More forward brow and forehead projection
Brow lift, forehead contouring, supraorbital implants, cranioplasty

paras: The brow ridge is a bony crest on the frontal bone above the eye sockets, separating the forehead from the roof of the orbits. The eyebrows sit along its lower margin, and the two ridges meet at the smooth glabella, behind which lie the frontal sinuses.[10] Brow ridges are usually more pronounced in men than women and vary across populations, which is why they feature in anthropological work on sexual dimorphism.[10]

Anthropologists offer several explanations for the ridge: a spatial model in which it forms between the growing face and braincase, a biomechanical model tied to chewing forces, and a protective role for the eyes.[10] In facial feminization writing, male eyebrows typically sit at or below the ridge while female eyebrows sit above it.[5]

In paediatric surgery, fronto-orbital advancement moves the supraorbital bar and frontal bone forward, with Wikipedia citing a target position about 3 mm in front of the corneas and advancements typically of 7 to 15 mm.[2] It is usually performed between six and twelve months of age, when bone is more pliable, and in metopic or coronal synostosis it is combined with graft or bone-movement steps.[2] Documented risks include substantial bleeding and migration of titanium plates as bone remodels, so absorbable plates are now preferred.[2] The operation aims at normal cranial development rather than at adult cosmetic projection.[2]

subs.h: Frontal bossing as a medical sign
paras: Frontal bossing is described as a protuberance of the skull, most often of the frontal bones, and is linked to excess growth hormone in acromegaly, rickets, beta-thalassaemia and other conditions of increased marrow activity, and numerous genetic syndromes.[3] In acromegaly the forehead and overlying skin thicken, which can produce bossing along with a widened nose and prominent cheekbones.[4]

Fronto-orbital advancement carries a clinical meaning tied to infant skull development, and frontal bossing is a sign that clinicians read as a symptom of an underlying condition, so the cosmetic use of both terms in forums is an adaptation of medical vocabulary rather than the name of an established cosmetic operation.[2][3] Medical sources describe the infant operation as moving a bone segment about 3 mm in front of the corneas with advancements typically of 7 to 15 mm, and list substantial bleeding and migration of titanium plates among documented risks.[2]

sections.h: Why the brow ridge is studied
paras: Anthropologists have proposed that the brow ridge reflects the spatial relationship between the orbit and the brain case, with researchers such as Moss and Young (1960) arguing it forms as the face advances forward during growth, and a biomechanical line of work by Endo, Russell and others tying ridge size to chewing forces and facial projection [10]. In 2015 Carrier and Morgan suggested that the ridge's sexual dimorphism fits a protective role for the eyes in combat [10]. Fossil evidence indicates early modern humans such as those at Jebel Irhoud had thick ridges, and that the ridge reduced in later hominins as the cranial vault grew and the forehead became more vertical [10].

These sources are why looksmaxxing discussions frame brow projection as a dimorphic trait: it tends to be stronger in men, is easiest to see in profile, and is read as part of the visual signal of sex [10].

sections.h: Conditions that produce a prominent forehead
paras: Medical sources describe frontal bossing as an unusually pronounced forehead that may come with a heavier brow ridge. It occurs when the frontal bone enlarges, often alongside other facial, skull, jaw and hand and foot bones, as in acromegaly, or when expanded bone marrow in chronic anaemia enlarges skull cavities [3]. Associated conditions listed include rickets, beta-thalassaemia, achondroplasia, Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes and several other genetic disorders [3]. These are clinical findings tied to underlying disease, which is why surgeons and endocrinologists treat the sign differently from an aesthetic preference [3][4].

sections.h: History of forehead surgery for appearance
paras: Cosmetic forehead surgery developed mainly through facial feminization. Wikipedia dates the first consideration of the field to 1982, when surgeon Darrell Pratt asked Douglas Ousterhout to operate on a transgender woman's face; Ousterhout later tested skull measurements to see which features reliably distinguish male from female and is credited with pioneering most of the procedures [5]. Forehead cranioplasty was discussed in the literature in 2011, and the same article describes hairline lowering and scalp advancement as related forehead work [5]. Brow-lift surgery has an older history, beginning with Erich Lexer in 1910.

Facial feminization surgery is a group of procedures that change male facial features toward female ones, performed mainly on transgender women.[6] For the forehead, surgeons grind down the solid part of the ridge, and where the bone over the frontal sinus is thin they either shave and smooth with bone cement or perform cranioplasty, reattaching reshaped bone with titanium wires or plates.[5] Wikipedia states there is not enough data to say which approach is better, and lists risks including breakthrough into the sinus, poor bone healing, fragment movement and cyst formation.[5]

A forehead or brow lift elevates a drooping eyebrow or smooths forehead lines. It was first discussed medically by Erich Lexer in 1910, and techniques include endoscopic, coronal, direct, temporal, pretrichial and transblepharoplasty approaches. Botulinum toxin is also used to raise the brow by relaxing the muscles that pull it down.[7] These change soft-tissue position rather than bone projection.

Because bone advancement is a major operation, people interested in the brow area also discuss changes that alter how the eye region reads without moving bone. Brow lifts reposition the eyebrow and upper lid skin, and botulinum toxin lifts the lateral brow by weakening the muscles that pull it down; a 2000 case series examined this brow elevation, and later series report outcomes and complications for endoscopic and direct brow lifts.[7][8][9] Under-eye support, maxillary projection and fat grafting are the other levers members name for the same eye-area look.[1]

Where bone-level change is sought, the published surgical literature centres on reconstruction rather than elective enhancement. A 2024 systematic review in Frontiers in Surgery by Kauke-Navarro and colleagues examined hydroxyapatite implants and cements for facial skeletal work and identified 12 studies covering 74 patients, published between 1997 and 2024.[11] Only one of those studies addressed the frontal region; four addressed the orbit, including the supraorbital rim, two the mandible and five several regions.[11]

The reviewers described hydroxyapatite as biocompatible and osteoconductive, with reported bony ingrowth, and noted a general trend toward positive outcomes, while pointing out that aesthetic results were mostly judged subjectively and that nine of the twelve studies were low-level (level IV) evidence with short follow-up.[11] Eight of the twelve studies reported no complications; the others described intraoperative fractures of patient-specific implants in four of 13 patients in one study, one implant removed for exposure, and, in orbital reconstructions, tear-sac infection, drooping eyelid and persistent eye-position problems in a minority of patients.[11] The authors also note the material is brittle and has low mechanical strength, which limits its use in load-bearing areas.[11]

These findings relate to reconstruction of defects and to implants generally. The review does not evaluate a procedure whose purpose is to move a healthy brow ridge forward, and forum discussion of supraorbital implants or bone cement for that purpose rests on individual surgeons' practice and members' accounts rather than published comparative series.[11][1]

No studies found on cosmetic forward advancement of the brow and orbit for appearance. Related published work concerns brow lifts, including a prospective case series of 22 patients on botulinum toxin brow elevation,[7] a personal review of 538 patients undergoing endoscopic brow lift with different fixation techniques,[8] and a study of the direct brow lift's efficacy, complications and patient satisfaction.[9] A review of facial feminization surgery covers the reverse goal of reducing brow projection.[6]

Looksmax.org members post about brow lifts, often as part of combined surgery packages abroad with other procedures such as genioplasty, cheek implants and canthopexy. These threads concern brow-lift surgery and recovery rather than bone advancement.

A separate thread argues that under-eye support from a forward and upward maxilla, not a forward brow, produces the hunter-eye look, and that working on the brow risks an 'ogre' appearance; a reply counters that straight forward supraorbital ridges matter most.[1] Members use terms such as supraorbital implants and under-eye fat grafts in these discussions.[1]

Members describe the eye area as a combination of brow ridge, orbital rim, upper-lid exposure and maxillary support, and threads on the topic frequently disagree about which element is the limiting factor.[1] The term frontal bossing also circulates as a joke on bodybuilding forums, where members tease each other about growth-hormone use changing their foreheads, a reference to the thickened forehead and skin seen in acromegaly.[12][4]

Because no standard elective operation exists for projecting the brow of someone with a healthy forehead, accounts in these communities of supraorbital implants, bone cement or custom implants describe individual surgeons' work rather than an established, published technique [1][11].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the forward brow is discussed alongside orbital support and midface position as a component of the hunter-eye look; threads disagree about which feature matters most.[1] T Nation members use frontal bossing mainly as a joke about growth hormone.[12]
